Merge-lane ratchet, the TESTS-map arm (measured 2026-09-12 at HEAD=e9d1055ed8, task 5097 planning). Complements the earlier entry on cluster TOTALS and complexipy charging; this is the rule that bites a task adding TEST coverage rather than source.

scripts/merge_lane_metrics.py::test_file_measures admits an orchestrator/tests file to the baseline's `tests` map iff `imports_lane_module(source)` — i.e. it imports orchestrator.merge_queue, orchestrator.merge_lane, or any other CLUSTER_PATHS module. Consequences for a NEW test file:
- It gains a `tests` entry, which ALONE stales the committed baseline and reddens test_baseline_matches_a_fresh_measurement (byte-identity).
- Its private_reads feed derive_totals, which sums the WHOLE current tests map (baseline 7847 over 229 entries) and _check_totals fails on any rise. _check_tests iterates BASELINE keys only and skips absent paths, so the per-file arm does NOT protect you — the totals arm does the failing. The ratchet's own seeded self-test pins a brand-new file with private_reads:1 as a total:private_reads violation.
- private_reads is deliberately RECEIVER-AGNOSTIC: any `x._foo` (non-dunder) counts, including writes (`worker._host_allocator = a`) and calls (`await worker._dispatch_item(i)`), and chains count per hop. Bare self./cls. receivers are excluded, but `self.worker._x` counts. No helper, fixture or naming trick avoids it.
- patch_targets is a UNION across all tests entries, so reusing a leaf already in the baseline's 83 is free; a brand-new leaf is a violation.

Practical upshot: a test file that imports only orchestrator.verify_runner or orchestrator.config is INVISIBLE to both gates (neither is a cluster path) and can use unrestricted private access and length. orchestrator/tests/test_host_allocator.py is the worked example — absent from the baseline, module-level imports are pytest only. Keep new merge-lane-adjacent tests lane-import-free on purpose when you can.

When you genuinely cannot test the wiring (e.g. a new config knob threaded into merge_queue.py), pyright is the available substitute: orchestrator/pyproject.toml [tool.pyright] includes both `src` and `tests`, so making the new parameter REQUIRED keyword-only turns an unwired call site into a reportCallIssue on every pre-commit and verify. Task 5097 took that route after confirming no test anywhere drives the real SpeculativeMergeWorker._dispatch_item.

Also measured: merge_queue.py sits at EXACTLY its frozen lines=21572 / prose_lines=12288 / cognitive=2132, so a task that adds no cluster file has ZERO line slack there and must make every comment/docstring edit line-count-preserving (E501 is ignored in orchestrator/pyproject.toml, so a long line needs no wrap). Such a task raises no measure and must therefore NOT regenerate the baseline — regeneration is only correct for a commit that legitimately changes a measure (e.g. ζ1's new package directory).

entry_text: Scheduler test gotcha (orchestrator/src/orchestrator/scheduler.py): when acquire_next has an EMPTY candidate pool, the tick ends at the empty_candidate_gate phase BEFORE the pin phase (_phase_select_pins) runs. Anything the pin phase does is therefore skipped on such a tick: pin reservation bound/release, pin_blocked, head reservation. A test that makes the only pending pin ineligible (e.g. status 'blocked') and expects the pin phase to react must keep at least one other pending candidate in the task list (e.g. a free low-priority task). Found in task 6040; the scheduler_tick event's terminal_phase field shows where a tick stopped.
target_text: DISCOVERY (dark-factory scheduler, verified in runs.db 2026-09-25): a dispatched task's fairness parks are NOT cleared at dispatch unless it is the scored loop's top_id. Scheduler._phase_select_pins never calls clear_parks_for, and _phase_select_scored clears parks only for top_id. So a pinned or non-top task keeps its park for its whole run, until Scheduler.release's 'defensive' clear_parks_for removes it silently (no reservation_used, no event). While it runs, that leftover park blocks same-tier park installs by other tasks (INV-3), producing PARTIAL installs. Measured since 2026-06-23: 466 full / 74 partial / 817 empty reservation_installed. The partials are concentrated in the critical+pinned group (3620, 3541, 3542, 4541). 44 dispatches kept their own park. Detect it: a lock_acquired with no preceding reservation_used, for a task with an active park, whose scheduler_tick has terminal_phase=select_pins.

target_text: Auditing delivered_checks / capability-manifest descriptors: the REFERENCE TREE is load-bearing and picking the wrong one inverts the result. A delivered_check is a forward-looking producer gate, so it is SUPPOSED to fail when written and pass after its producer lands. Evaluating the (expect x matches) 2x2 against MAIN TODAY therefore misreads every successfully-delivered done check as "vacuous" — measured on dark_factory at HEAD f38463508e (52 manifests, 548 verdict-PASS kind=grep descriptors) that flags 313/548 (57%), versus 104/538 (19%) when evaluated against each manifest's own authoring tree. Rules of thumb: (1) at AUTHORING time the reference tree is free — HEAD is the pre-task tree, so a vacuity gate there needs no git history at all; (2) retroactively you cannot recover the authoring tree without a commit-ordering premise, so a retroactive sweep must be STATUS-AWARE (present+no-match is a defect on a done task and healthy on a pending one), which means tasks.db and therefore scripts/, not the shared test suite; (3) never assert a corpus-wide vacuity count in a pytest gate — it is un-greenable and the population drifts.

The dark_factory memory-consolidation gate treadmill is a MISSING-PRIMITIVE problem, not a curator-judgment problem. Established 2026-07-31 by code audit.

The landed policy (task 2805, `fused-memory/src/fused_memory/reconciliation/recon_self_model.py:568-586`, rendered into both Stage-1 and Stage-2 prompts, from `plans/operational-ask-routing-prd.md` §Resolved-4) says: merge exact/near-exact duplicates inline — "the safe, **reversible-enough** consolidation" — but escalate any content-losing or irreversible judgment call as a human gate. Its out-of-scope bullet makes that boundary deliberate and permanent-by-intent.

**Nothing in this subsystem is reversible**, so that predicate routes almost everything to a human:
- No in-place update on the MCP surface. `update_memory` does not exist as a tool; the backend primitive `Mem0Backend.update` (`backends/mem0_client.py:238-262`) has exactly one caller, a script. Task 3055 (the decision) is done; **task 3088 (the implementation) is pending**. So consolidation MUST be delete+rewrite — precisely the irreversible content-losing operation the policy says to escalate.
- `delete_memory` records ids only, no content, no undo (`memory_service.py:3470-3529`). 200–370 deletions/day.
- 0 of 119 cited consolidation sources still exist in the collection — every merge is unauditable from the store afterwards.
- A soft-blocked write is recorded NOWHERE: no journal row, event, log or counter (`near_duplicate_guard.py` imports no logger); only `content[:200]` returns to the caller. The guard's false-positive rate is therefore unmeasurable after the fact.
- No structured provenance: no `consolidated_from`/`supersedes` key exists anywhere in `fused_memory/`; survivor↔source linkage is LLM prose inside `content`.
- THREE incompatible definitions of "duplicate": 0.92 cosine top-5 same-project/category (write guard), 0.85 lexical `difflib.SequenceMatcher` all-corpus (`scripts/audit_duplicate_memories.py`), and LLM judgment (Stage 1).
- `pick_survivor` in the offline sweep keeps the OLDEST absent a canonical flag — while in every open gate the NEWEST entry is the one carrying the new detail.
- Stage 1's tool access is a DENY-list only, so it holds `delete_memory`, `delete_entity`, `merge_entities`, `rename_entity`, `set_entity_summary`.

The guard's own remediation hint tells agents to "search first and **update** or skip" — an operation the MCP surface cannot perform.

IMPLICATION: adding (a) a content-preserving delete, (b) one journal row on soft-block, and (c) task 3088's in-place update would make most of these gates mechanically safe to close without a human — because consolidation would stop being irreversible, which is the only reason the policy escalates them.

entry_text: reify-lsp gotcha: `DocumentState::parsed_module` (crates/reify-lsp/src/document.rs) holds its `parsed_cache` Mutex across `parse_with_stdlib` ON PURPOSE. That makes it a single-flight memo: concurrent same-version callers wait for the ONE in-flight parse of identical text and then get the same Arc. Moving the parse outside the lock with a CAS-style install cannot lower any caller's latency. A latecomer would wait a full parse P instead of the remaining P−t, and the change would add up to (N−1) duplicate parses of CPU. The real per-keystroke redundancy is elsewhere: didChange's diagnostics parse (diagnostics.rs `compute_diagnostics_with_state`) is never shared into the DocumentState cache. (Analysis from task 7272's architect pass, not a benchmark.)
target_text: reify-lsp now caches the user-document parse per document version. `DocumentState` (document.rs) holds `parsed_cache: Mutex<Option<Arc<ParsedModule>>>` filled lazily by `parsed_module(ModulePath) -> Arc<ParsedModule>` (poison-recovering lock). `DocumentStore::get` returns `Option<Arc<DocumentState>>`. Every server.rs provider (hover, goto-def, completion, document_symbol, document_highlight, prepare_rename, rename) fetches the Arc<DocumentState>, drops the ServerState read lock, then parses OFF the lock via `doc.parsed_module(mp)` — goto_definition moves the Arc into spawn_blocking so the parse runs on the blocking pool. Cache invalidation is structural: did_open/did_change install a fresh DocumentState with an empty cache (no version-compare). hover/completion build `AnalysisContext::from_parsed(arc)` (compile+check stay per-request); the others use the `*_with_parsed` / `*_in_context` / `compute_document_symbols_from_parsed` cores. The stdlib/prelude side was already process-globally memoized inside `parse_with_stdlib` (OnceLock), so no new global cache was added.

entry_text: `reify check` (cmd_check, crates/reify-cli/src/main.rs ~815) exits FAILURE on ANY compile-time Error diagnostic before it evaluates constraints, so it never prints per-constraint OK/INDETERMINATE lines for a file with a compile Error. A PRD signal that wants both a new compile Error and an "X still reports OK" line on the same file therefore cannot be met at the CLI. Assert the "still OK" half on the compiler surface (constraint generated) or by calling Engine::check directly on the compiled module. Also measured 2026-10-02: an ad-hoc `connect a @ point(..) -> b @ point(..)` frame_align is permanently Indeterminate because reify-expr eval_eq has no Value::Frame arm.
target_text: In reify, `reify check` DOES gate on compile-layer diagnostics but NOT on build/realization ones: `cmd_check` (crates/reify-cli/src/main.rs ~776-782) returns ExitCode::FAILURE on any compile `Severity::Error` and short-circuits BEFORE constraint checking and before `build()`, so a compile error suppresses the `OK <id>` / `All constraints satisfied.` stdout entirely; realization-only errors (e.g. `failed to compile geometry operation: ...`) still print on stderr with exit 0 until task 5403 lands PRD 2's general Severity::Error exit gate. Measured 2026-08-30 at main 2227f36c4d: `box(20, 20, 10)` -> exit 1 with three ArgTypeMismatch errors and no constraint output; `mirror(arm, 0,0,0, 1,0,0)` -> exit 0 with the same-worded error on stderr. Re-measured 2026-09-01 on branch task/5662 with the same builtin family: `mirror(g, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0)` (compile tier) -> exit 1, EMPTY stdout, no verdict line at all; `mirror(g, plane_yz(0))` (build tier) -> exit 0, with "All constraints satisfied." printed BENEATH three ArgTypeMismatch errors on stderr. Consequence: adding a compile-layer `CheckableArg` slot for a builtin used by any reify-cli negative fixture silently flips that fixture's `reify check` exit code and hides its build-layer diagnostics — and conversely, never claim in docs or tests that a build-tier error "does not appear under check" or is "build-only": it does appear, on stderr. Always read check's stderr and never trust its exit code alone.

GOTCHA that misreads the orchestrator xdist "worker crashed" recipe (measured 2026-09-06, task 4384): a `@pytest.mark.timeout(N)` marker OVERRIDES the `--timeout=...` on the command line, so the merge-verify test_command's `--timeout=300` is NOT the effective per-test budget for any test or module carrying its own marker.

MEASURED, not inferred: a probe `@pytest.mark.timeout(2)` sleeping 5s, run with `--timeout=300`, failed with `Failed: Timeout (>2.0s) from pytest-timeout` in 2.11s. Corroborated in the installed pytest_timeout.py: `_get_item_settings` returns the marker's parsed settings and never consults ini/CLI when a marker is present.

WHY IT MATTERS. When triaging `worker 'gwNN' crashed while running '<test>'` you will reach for the verify command to find the budget the test blew. That number is usually wrong. Read the marker instead — `pytest.mark.timeout` on the function, or a module-level `pytestmark`. Worked example: test_aiosqlite_leak_isolation.py::test_a_thread_exception_actually_fails_a_test_under_this_projects_inifile carries `@pytest.mark.timeout(120)` while merge-verify passes `--timeout=300`; its real budget is 120s. It spawns two nested pytest subprocesses and measured 18.5s solo / 26.9s inside a green full suite, so under load-driven slowdown it can cross 120s — where the ini's `timeout_method="thread"` `os._exit()`s the worker and `--max-worker-restart=0` (task 1907) escalates that one worker death into a whole-session `triggershutdown()` (xdist/dsession.py:256). Observed shape: the run stops at ~1-2% with "1 failed, N passed" out of ~20k collected.

CONTRAST worth knowing when judging whether a blamed test is a random bystander: the repo's sanctioned heavy-test family ceiling is `WHOLE_TREE_SCAN_TEST_TIMEOUT = 5 * PYPROJECT_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` = 300s (_orch_helpers.py:163, task 4215), applied as a module-level pytestmark. A heavy subprocess-spawning test sitting at 120s has materially less headroom than that family, so it is a likelier repeat offender than a truly random test — check the marker before concluding "random innocent bystander".

This REFINES, and does not replace, the existing diagnostic recipe (rerun in isolation → rerun the file → rerun the full suite and see whether a DIFFERENT test is blamed; do not xfail/skip the blamed test; do not loosen timeouts or --max-worker-restart as a task-scoped fix). That recipe's remedy still held here: three reruns green, full suite 20359 passed in 26:46 at loadavg ~110, zero code changes.

target_text: Reify GUI Lezer grammar, two facts that refine the existing "the editor is a subset, so the editor yields" rule (memories 1da8ce4b, d3b7d720 — both framed only as "never make the editor MORE expressive than the compiler"). (1) The divergence can run the OTHER way, and then the editor must be WIDENED, not left alone: measured on task 5495, `sub h : pp.Pulley<T>` parsed clean in tree-sitter-reify/grammar.js and lowered to a valid SubDecl with no diagnostic, while gui/src/editor/reify.grammar produced 2 error nodes — the editor STRICTER than the compiler, which red-underlines valid source in the editor and is just as much a divergence. Fix shape that worked: attach the optional type-arg tail at the SLOT (`subSpecializedName { ParameterizedType | NamespacedName ("<" TypeArgList ">")? | Identifier }`), never on the shared name rule itself, which keeps node names stable and mirrors how upstream spells it. Gotcha for shell wrappers that source a sibling lib (task 5158): locate it with fork-free parameter expansion `case "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" in */*) d="${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}";; *) d=.;; esac`, never `$(dirname ...)` or `$REPO`.
- dirname: the uv-wrapper tests run under an EMPTY PATH, so `$(dirname ...)` yields "" and the source silently becomes /lib/....
- $REPO: fused-memory/scripts/cgl_eta_auto_apply.sh hardcodes REPO to the MAIN checkout, so a worktree would source main's copy.
- `${0##*/}` is the fork-free basename for ERROR prefixes, and `$0` inside `$(...)` is still the caller's path.
target_text: A bash script that resolves its own directory with `$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)` is silently PATH-DEPENDENT, and its failure is a wrong answer rather than an error: `dirname` is an external binary, so under a PATH that lacks it the command substitution yields EMPTY, `cd ""` succeeds as a no-op, and the script dir resolves to the CALLER'S CWD. Measured on dark-factory task 3074 (orchestrator/scripts/warm-lane/lib_lane_state.sh) — a test that replaced PATH wholesale with a stub bin dir hit exactly this, and the repo root came back as the CWD's grandparent. Use parameter expansion instead, with the no-slash guard: `dir='.'; case "$src" in */*) dir="${src%/*}"; [ -n "$dir" ] || dir='/';; esac` — `cd` and `pwd` are builtins, so the arithmetic then needs nothing on PATH. This is a caveat ON, not a replacement for, the nested-dirname depth convention (memory 877f4630) and the prefer-arithmetic-over-`git rev-parse` finding (915eae1a): both are about WHICH path you compute; this is about the fork used to compute it. Corollary: never leave a `${DIR:-.}` fallback in the ascent — it answers *something* for every input, which is what makes a "could not resolve" branch unreachable and lets a wrong root look like a right one.

The backlog path uses MemoryService.search, which is ALSO ungrouped. server/grouped_read.py's own LAYERING CONSTRAINT docstring says the child-suppression filter is called ONLY from the MCP tool wrappers and that MemoryService.search is deliberately NOT touched — precisely so children stay visible to reconciliation/mem0_dedup.py and the near-duplicate write guard. (2) TRIAGE IS ADD-ONLY AND RETROACTIVELY INERT. server/write_triage.py: triage issues no update_memory and no delete_memory, never edits a canonical. The existing duplicate population that generates today's gates carries no parent_id and is untouched by the flip.

FOURTH proof needed for a df_pytest_isolation suite-wide fixture, extending memory 2d41742b's three (marker pin / getfixturevalue / nested-run). Those three all run inside ONE test root and therefore cannot see a defect whose precondition is TWO roots' instances being live in ONE session — which is what task 4398 was.

THE DEFECT CLASS. `_df_fleet_dir_redirect` is session-scoped AND autouse, and each root's conftest binds its OWN copy (conftest.py, scripts/tests/conftest.py, orchestrator/tests/conftest.py). Sibling conftests produce distinct FixtureDefs with independent caches, so a session collecting two roots runs BOTH instances. Each unconditionally mktemp'd a dir and overwrote os.environ, so the root whose fixture ran FIRST kept yielding a path the env var no longer held, and its per-root identity assertion failed. Reachable only from the ordinary both-roots command (scripts/orchestrator.yaml's test_command); a scoped run of either root alone stays green, and so does every pure-helper unit test of the rule the fixture consumes.

THE PROOF SHAPE (tests/scripts/test_fleet_dir_isolation.py::TestTheAdoptBranchHoldsInARealSession). Extend the existing nested-pytest idiom to TWO SUB-ROOTDIRS under one nested root: `root_a/conftest.py` and `root_b/conftest.py` each `from df_pytest_isolation import _df_fleet_dir_redirect  # noqa: F401` (sys.path.insert of `Path(__file__).parent.parent`, since the copied module sits in the nested root). Each nested test takes the fixture BY NAME and RECORDS what it yielded plus the env var it saw, to a file the outer test reads. The outer test then asserts the two roots agree on ONE directory AND that it is what the env var held. Order the modules A, B, A on the command line to reproduce the original report exactly — but do NOT make the assertions depend on that order: comparing the two roots' RECORDED paths discriminates regardless of collection order, which is the property that keeps the test from going quietly vacuous if pytest ever reorders.

TWO THINGS THAT MAKE IT WORK, both non-obvious. (1) The nested session INHERITS the outer session's ORCH_FLEET_DIR, which points into the OUTER basetemp — so the first instance correctly REFUSES it (a previous run's value is not adoptable) and creates, and only the second adopts. You get the create path and the adopt path in one run, in production order, for free. (2) Give the three nested modules DISTINCT basenames; the nested run has no `--import-mode=importlib` (its pytest.ini is a bare `[pytest]`), so same-named modules in sibling dirs without `__init__.py` collide.

VALIDATE IT BY MUTATION, per memory f3541b8e's lesson. Stub the helper the branch consumes to `return None` (adoption disabled) and confirm the nested run reproduces the ORIGINAL report: measured `fleet-dir0 != fleet-dir1` under one basetemp at `root_a/test_a_second`, which is verbatim what 4398 named. A nested test that passes both with and without the branch is the dead defence this whole family exists to detect.

entry_text: When re-planning a reify task branch that has diverged from main, preview the conflicts without touching the lane with `git merge-tree --write-tree --name-only main HEAD` (git 2.43). Exit 1 means conflicts: the first line is the merged tree OID, and the conflicted paths follow. Hunks can be read via `git ls-tree -r <oid> <path>` plus `git cat-file -p <blob>`. A conflict where main edited PROSE inside a section the branch MOVED to another file resolves textually to the branch side, but git cannot carry main's edit to the destination file. Port it by hand, as task 6956 did with #7063's helpers.rs wording moving into harness_doc_chunks/module_compile.rs.
target_text: To decide rebase-vs-merge (or size the conflict cost) for a stale reify task branch WITHOUT touching the working tree, run `git merge-tree --write-tree main HEAD` (git 2.43 in-tree). It prints the merged tree OID, then the auto-merge/CONFLICT lines per path, and `git cat-file -p "<tree>:<path>"` yields the conflict-marked file so you can read the exact hunks before committing to anything. This is safe to run while a `cargo test` is in flight, unlike `git merge --no-commit`. Prefer `git merge main` over `git rebase main` on a task branch: a rebase rewrites every commit SHA and destroys the `mark_step_committed` provenance in `.task/plan.json`. Merging main into a task branch is established in-repo practice (e.g. `Merge main into task/4880`, `Merge main into task/6211`, `Merge branch 'main' into task/5627`). With CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN set, the env token is used even when the file is garbage, empty or half-written, and a garbage env token fails with 401 over a valid file. target_text:
When probing whether a Claude Max OAuth account is alive, run a DELIBERATELY BOGUS token first as a negative control, in an ISOLATED config dir. Established 2026-09-01 while verifying max-h.

Why the control is load-bearing: `_run_probe`'s command falls back to ambient Claude CLI credentials whenever the token plumbing silently fails to take. Without a control, a passing probe is indistinguishable from "the CLI quietly used Leo's own logged-in credentials", which would certify a dead account as healthy. The control run must FAIL — with a bogus 108-char `sk-ant-oat01-XXXX…` token it returned rc=1 and `result: "Failed to authenticate. API Error: 401 OAuth access token is invalid."` at cost $0. Only then does the real run mean anything.

Why the isolated dir is load-bearing: the probe writes `.credentials.json` into `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`. Pointing that at the default would CLOBBER Leo's own interactive credentials (max-a). Mirror `shared/src/shared/config_dir.py::TaskConfigDir.write_credentials` into a fresh `tempfile.mkdtemp()` — write `{"claudeAiOauth": {"accessToken": <token>}}`, `chmod 0o600` — set `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` to it, and `shutil.rmtree` it afterwards.

Also strip `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the probe env (as production does). Leaving it in lets the CLI bill the API directly and succeed even with a dead OAuth token — a second route to a false positive, and it silently moves spend off the Max subscription.

Reading the verdict itself is a separate, already-documented matter: `subtype: "error_max_budget_usd"` is the NORMAL success outcome, not a failure.

target_text:
MEASURED 2026-09-15 (task 5319, in worktree .worktrees/5319, httpx 0.28.1 / httpcore 1.0.9): httpcore's connection pool CAN retain a connection that no reaping branch will ever reclaim. This does NOT contradict the task-3857 refutations (mem0 eb3c5348 of 2026-08-08 and ce1fd1f7 of 2026-08-17) — it names the case neither measured, and both remain correct inside their scope.

THE BOUNDARY. AsyncConnectionPool._assign_requests_to_connections reclaims on exactly three predicates: is_closed(), has_expired(), is_idle()-and-surplus. In AsyncHTTP11Connection, is_closed() is _state==CLOSED, is_idle() is _state==IDLE, and has_expired() is (_expire_at set and passed) OR (_state==IDLE and socket readable). _expire_at is set to None on entry to ACTIVE and only re-armed by _response_closed(). So a connection parked in NEW or ACTIVE satisfies NONE of the three, while is_available() (IDLE-only) makes it unusable. It holds a pool slot forever and its socket forever. ce1fd1f7's finding (2) — "cleanup runs BEFORE max_connections is evaluated, so a CLOSE-WAIT socket cannot hold a slot permanently" — is true only for connections the cleanup pass can SEE, i.e. IDLE ones. Its finding (3) is the reason why: the server-disconnect term is gated on _state==IDLE.

HOW ONE GETS PARKED. AsyncHTTP11Connection.handle_async_request sets _state = ACTIVE OUTSIDE its try block, and AsyncHTTPConnection's `except BaseException: self._connect_failed = True` is consulted by the predicates ONLY when self._connection is None — once _connect() has succeeded that flag is dead weight. A cancellation landing in that window, or inside the AsyncShieldCancellation-wrapped _response_closed() cleanup (anyio's shield does not stop a plain-asyncio task.cancel()), parks the connection.

WHY 15/15 CANCELLED PROBES SAW NOTHING. The window is a few event-loop steps wide. A single sequential cancelled probe essentially never lands in it; that measurement is sound and its conclusion ("do not attribute CLOSE-WAIT growth to wait_for cancellation without measuring") stays good advice. Reproducing it needs either concurrency plus randomized deadlines (found it at conc=10 over ~20 rounds against a loopback asyncio.start_server, two stuck states: "HTTP/1.1, ACTIVE, Request Count: 1" and "HTTP/1.1, NEW, Request Count: 0"), or determinism.

HOW TO REPRODUCE DETERMINISTICALLY — no sockets, no wall clock, no flake. Build httpx.AsyncClient over an httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport whose _pool you replace with httpcore.AsyncConnectionPool(network_backend=<fake>); the fake AsyncNetworkBackend/AsyncNetworkStream buffers a canned response on write and drains it on read. Start client.post as a task, step the loop exactly k times with `await asyncio.sleep(0)`, then task.cancel(). Sweep k: on these versions k=3 mints a NEW-state orphan with its stream unclosed, and three subsequent successful POSTs through the same pool do NOT reclaim it. Sweep k rather than pinning it — the number is a property of the dependency's yield schedule, not of the defect.

THE SOUND DETECTOR, if you need one. pool._requests holds the live AsyncPoolRequests and every abandonment path removes the request before letting go of the connection, so: orphan := in pool._connections AND not in {r.connection for r in pool._requests} AND neither is_idle() nor is_closed(). No timestamps, no grace period, and a genuinely in-flight request can never match.

A sleeper_spec-style test build therefore ends up as ONE process (a direct child of the verify-merge leader, leading its own session under start_new_session), not bash->sleep. target_text: Gotcha, measured 2026-09-29 for task 6029. On this host /bin/sh is dash 0.5.12, which FORKS the command for `sh -c 'sleep 30'` rather than exec'ing it. So asyncio.create_subprocess_shell(..., start_new_session=True) makes a group of the sh leader plus a sleep child. After the leader is killed and reaped, the child is orphaned to systemd --user (pid 2626) and sits in state R/Z. os.kill/os.killpg(..., 0) keeps succeeding until systemd --user reaps it. systemd --user was observed stalling for ~100s (2026-09-28 22:29:20 to 22:31:03 BST, with `systemctl --user show` timing out), so ANY bounded poll on killpg/kill(…,0) after killing a tree can false-red regardless of its timeout. That is what reddened test_proc_group's terminate tests after tasks 1081/1450 had "fixed" them with a 5s poll. Judge termination by /proc state instead (Z/X counts as exited). A deterministic zombie for tests: Popen, then SIGKILL, then os.waitid(P_PID, pid, WEXITED|WNOWAIT), which blocks until the child has exited without reaping it.

orchestrator/tests/_merge_lane_fakes.py gained the shared way to drive a merge lane in tests (task 5034).
- merge_through_lane(lane, queue, request, timeout=...) runs the lane, submits a single or train request through the lane's own queue, returns the MergeOutcome, and stops the lane.
- running_lane(lane) is an async context manager yielding a LaneRun. Use it for multi-submission tests. On exit it stops the lane and awaits run() unsuppressed, so a lane crash raises instead of being swallowed.
- LaneRun.outcome(request) waits on {run task, request.result}, so a lane that dies first surfaces as a crash, not as a TimeoutError.
- times_out() sits next to passes(), fails() and raises().

The reviewer had found that the first version of merge_through_lane suppressed BaseException on the run() task, which turned a crashing lane into a bare 120s TimeoutError. Do not write per-file create_task(lane.run()) / stop() lifecycles; use running_lane.
target_text:
MERGE-LANE TESTS — GATING an injected collaborator subclass, the deterministic way to observe a lane timing window. Extends the task-5031 amendment (7691ba5e, under 66fb4013), which established that a FakeVerifier SUBCLASS overriding a port method beats a monkeypatch and costs the ratchet nothing. Two increments, both measured on task 5461.

INCREMENT 1 — the technique is not limited to Protocol PORTS. `git_ops` is a CONCRETE class (`orchestrator.git_ops.GitOps`) passed as a constructor parameter of `MergeLane`, so a plain subclass overriding a PUBLIC method is the same seam: no `patch`, no `setattr`, no private read. test_merge_queue_metrics.py stayed at its baseline `{"patch_targets": [], "private_reads": 0}` with the subclass in the file (confirmed by `scripts/merge_lane_metrics.py --check` exiting 0). `self._gated_branch` on the subclass is free — the instrument exempts the bare `self` receiver.

INCREMENT 2 — the subclass can GATE, not just observe, and that is what buys DETERMINISM. Override the public method to `self.at_gate.set()` then `await self.release_merge.wait()` for ONE branch, and fall through to `super()` otherwise. This converts a few-awaits-wide internal window into a state the test holds open indefinitely. Concretely: the lane calls `_note_merge_started(req)` (stashing the drift base at the current main_position) immediately before `merge_to_main`, so parking INSIDE `merge_to_main` makes `at_gate` being set PROOF the base was already stashed — the test can then drive an unrelated request all the way to a landing, confirm it on the public counter, and only then release.

WHY IT MATTERS: the obvious alternative (submit both, poll `snapshot()['entries']` for the follower's state, release) was measured at 3 passes in 8 runs, with BOTH failure modes seen — drift 0 when the follower's speculative merge beat the landing, and the follower still `queued` at release time. The gated-merge drive measured 11/11 in probes and 5/5 as committed. Nothing in the public snapshot marks that window stably, so no amount of polling fixes the naive shape.

MANDATORY COMPANION: whatever helper starts the lane must release EVERY gate BEFORE `stop()` (see test_merge_queue_dispatch_fill_redispatch.py::_running_lane), or a failing assertion leaves a verify or a merge parked and hangs teardown instead of reporting. Extend the file's existing lane helper in place with keyword-only params defaulting to today's behaviour rather than adding a second lane-lifecycle helper.

Also note `speculation_depth` must be raised above the default `_MERGE_AHEAD_BOUND` (= 1) for any two-requests-in-flight drive: at depth 1 the lane never dequeues the second request while the first verifies, so its drift base is stashed AFTER the landing and the drift is 0 by construction.

target_text: Reify GUI: a Solid range input gives you the preview/commit split for free — its onInput fires per drag frame and its onChange fires once on pointer release. Solid's onChange is the NATIVE change event (no React-style change-to-input remapping), it is not in Solid's delegated-events set so it is bound with addEventListener, and fireEvent.change(slider, { target: { value } }) from @solidjs/testing-library reaches it. So binding two different IPC cadences to one slider needs no pointerdown/pointerup plumbing: MechanismPanel.tsx does exactly this — onInput schedules a RAF-coalesced transient preview_parameter, onChange issues the one durable set_parameter source write-back. Measured 2026-09-15, task 5099, warm lane _lane-24.

scripts/legibility/account_pool.py::pool_invoke catches only coder.CoderCapExhausted, which it rotates on a strict slot.detect_cap_hit, and treats an exit-0 unparseable banner as a cap. entry_text: faer 0.24 dense `gevd_real` (QZ) panics in reify DEBUG builds with 'attempt to subtract with overflow' at faer-0.24.0/src/linalg/gevd/qz_real/mod.rs:2287. Cause: aggressive_early_deflation sets `kwbot = kwtop.wrapping_sub(1)` (line 2222) when the deflation window starts at row 0, then computes `ihi - kwbot`. That wraps to the correct LAPACK value in release, but the generic QZ is monomorphised in reify-solver-elastic, which keeps dev overflow-checks on, so root `[profile.dev.package."*"]` overflow-checks=false does NOT help. Cheap reproducer: solve_eigen_dense on K=tridiag(-1,2,-1) n=136 with B tridiagonal (diag +1 for i<n/2, -0.5 after, off-diagonals 0.2). It passes with `cargo test --config 'profile.dev.package."reify-solver-elastic".overflow-checks=false'`. Task #7602 plans that profile override as the guard.

entry_text: Dashboard Tasks tab render cadence and layout cost (measured 2026-10-04, task 5116 architect). Since commit 6d5f7eedd8 the 1s wall clock lives in the app.jsx::LiveClock leaf, so TasksTab does NOT re-render every second. It re-renders on each data arrival (~20/min) and each interaction (node click, focus, filter). Any memo keyed on a per-render array (e.g. `[tasks]` from viewRows/filter/focusGroupView) still misses on all of those, and each poll replaces every row object, so only a content key hits. Measured with graph_layout.js under node on the live snapshot: one TaskGraph layout (computeTiers + partitionComponents + orderRows) costs 43.6ms for dark-factory (1,620 tasks) and 72.7ms avg / 161ms max for reify (1,657 tasks). target_text: The dark-factory dashboard's 1-second wall clock was, until 2026-09-23, responsible for roughly two thirds of its main-thread blocking — more than the 3-second data poll everyone assumed was the cost. app.jsx::App owned `setInterval(() => setNow(new Date()), 1000)` directly, so the whole tree including the active tab re-rendered about 60 times a minute against a data arrival rate of about 20, and React.memo appears NOWHERE in the dashboard bundle so nothing stopped it. Isolated experimentally on the Analytics tab in 25-second windows: polling on plus clock on = 14.4% of the main thread blocked; polling fully OFF (__DF_PAUSE, zero bytes arriving) plus clock on = 9.5%. Fixed in commit 6d5f7eedd8: the clock moved into a LiveClock leaf component that owns its own interval and renders only the timestamp, with StatStrip receiving that element instead of a string computed in App. Measured after the fix on the same tab, steady state with polling live: 6.4% blocked (44 long tasks, median 118ms, max 290ms, 89s window) — a cross-session comparison against the 14.4% baseline, so indicative rather than controlled, but the 60 removed full-tree renders per minute follow from the diff. The guard test test_tab_staleness_indicator.py::test_no_new_timer_is_introduced was inverted in the same commit: it previously asserted App() holds exactly ONE setInterval and now asserts zero in App(), exactly one in the file, and that one inside LiveClock — so hoisting a timer back into App() fails loudly.

entry_text: GOTCHA (merge-lane tests that pin a _disjoint_skip_blockers SKIP, measured task 5070 2026-10-03): a lane-scene OrchestratorConfig resolves merge_verify_breadth='full' (the live dark-factory-orchestrator.yaml is layered in; the Field default 'scoped' is not what the test sees), so P1 forces a re-verify and any mutation that empties the overlap delta SURVIVES. Pass merge_verify_breadth='scoped' explicitly and register the drift with note_queue_verified_main_tip. Also: GitOps.advance_main checks `merge-base --is-ancestor main <merge>` before update-ref, so a drift committed just BEFORE advance_main yields rebased_pending_reverify, never cas_failed. target_text: Task 2527 implemented the Coupling joint in crates/reify-stdlib/src/joints.rs. Key implementation decisions: (1) Coupling stored as Value::Map with 4 keys: kind="coupling", parent (full joint Map), ratio (Value::Real), offset (Value::Scalar typed to parent dimension). (5) joint_ratio and joint_offset accessors follow the same joint_axis/joint_range pattern (1-arg Map key lookup).

The fused-memory set_task_priority_override docstring overstates what pins and reserve_now do (fused-memory/src/fused_memory/server/tools.py). It says 'Pin this task to the front of the queue' and, for reserve_now, 'Reserve the next worker slot'.
In fact:
- A pin gives only a first try, each scheduler tick, at all-or-nothing module-lock acquisition, with no reservation.
- reserve_now installs parks once, at the task's RAW priority, and reserves no worker slot.
Operators pin expecting movement that the code does not provide. As of 2026-09-29 no task owns the docstring fix; it was deliberately kept out of 6040 to avoid adding a fused-memory file to it.

GOTCHA: a scheduler priority override (set_task_priority_override with boost_tier/pinned) is a NO-OP on a PARKED task, and the tool still returns success=True, so the failure is silent. Priority ordering only selects among DISPATCHABLE candidates; it cannot evict a module-lock holder. Measured 2026-08-07 stewarding task 3536: task 3248 was pinned to boost_tier=critical, pin_queue position 1 of 13, and still did not dispatch — it had been parked ~5.2h with skip_counts=14.

DIAGNOSE BEFORE PINNING. Call get_scheduler_state(project_root) and check, in order:
1. parks[task_id] — if present the task is lock-waiting, not merely low-priority. Its .modules is the requested module set and .installed_at gives the park age.
2. skip_counts[task_id] — a large value confirms the scheduler keeps passing it over.
3. Cross-reference every entry in parks[task_id].modules against current_holders. Usually only ONE entry is actually held; that single owner is the whole blocker. The other nine of ten being unheld is typical, so do not assume broad contention.
4. Check the holder's status and worktree mtime. If it is in-progress with a live worktree it is legitimate work — do NOT force-release its lock to unblock yours.

Locks are held at DIRECTORY granularity for package paths (e.g. fused-memory/src/fused_memory/middleware), so a one-line edit to a single file can be parked behind unrelated work touching any other file in that directory. That granularity is the usual cause of a surprising park, and it can invert priority: a bare-main-red fix blocking the whole merge lane can sit behind ordinary feature work indefinitely. When that happens the levers are to wait for the holder, land the change by the sanctioned direct-to-main route, or split the leaf into a task whose module set excludes the contended directory — not to pin harder.

Only a DUPLICATE label is diagnosed as a separate error; over-arity positional args take the same lenient `__arg{i}` fallback. So spelling every param out in declaration order is still good .ri style (it keeps a typo'd label visible under review, e.g. `element_order` quietly reverting to its P1 default) but is no longer required for correctness. CORRECTION/EXTENSION of memory ebdb01f8 (the "targeted.py passes no agent_id, and that is load-bearing" gotcha, task 4903 planning). That entry concludes the HUMAN-vs-RECONCILIATION classification is "legality-neutral today" because both unions admit (BLOCKED, PENDING). Measured during task 4903's amendment pass: that is true only of the status the write was DECIDED from, not of the status it lands on.

THE CONSEQUENCE THE NEUTRALITY CLAIM HIDES. ActorClass.RECONCILIATION's union subtracts every (in-progress, *) pair — that subtraction is the FSM-level guard stopping a reconciler from mutating a live, claimed task. With agent_id=None the write classifies HUMAN, the FULL _UNION is consulted, and (in-progress, pending) IS legal there. So a targeted.py sweep that decides "this task is blocked" from a get_tasks snapshot and writes later gets NO transition-table protection if the task left blocked in between — and blocked->in-progress is a legal edge (harness resume-at-verify). reconcile_task is fire-and-forget background work that can be scheduled arbitrarily late, and a sweep may do escalation-store I/O between snapshot and write, so that window is real, not theoretical. You cannot close it by passing a recon agent_id either: that re-arms ReconWritePolicy Gate 2, which refuses the write whenever the project-wide orchestrator lock is held (i.e. almost always). Both options are unavailable; the sweep must self-guard.

THE PATTERN. Any deterministic reconciler status write decided from a snapshot must re-read live status immediately before the write and skip if the status moved — targeted.py::_sweep_cancelled_descendants already does this with _live_status_map (lazily memoized once per sweep, tri-state list memo), and task 4903's _unblock_dependent adopted the same idiom, placing the re-read LAST (after the pure-metadata and escalation-pin vetoes) so the window is as small as possible. Fail direction on an unreadable re-read: skip, do not write.

ALSO: if a docstring claims a write "survives the ActorClass.RECONCILIATION restriction", check whether that class is actually derived for it. In targeted.py it never is, and the claim described a check that never ran.

GOTCHA (dark_factory, measured first-hand 2026-09-14, task 4887): wiring `delivered_checks=` into `validate_landing_evidence` is NOT an inert observability change — it ACTIVATES a previously-unreachable SECOND ACCEPT PATH and silently weakens what every `accepted` verdict from that call site guarantees. Any of tasks 4496 (harness.py) / 4497 (merge_queue.py) / 4500 (the required+keyword-only capstone) inherits this the moment it wires its own site.

THE MECHANISM. In `orchestrator/src/orchestrator/landing_evidence.py::validate_landing_evidence`, the second accept path sits INSIDE the `if not await git_ops.commit_effect_present_in_main(...)` branch, in BOTH modes (CANDIDATE `return _accept(candidate_sha)`, DISCOVERY `return _accept(citation)`), guarded by `if delivered_checks and await _delivered_checks_differential(...)`. So while a site passes the default, that branch is dead and every accept carries the full FIX 1' effect-present guarantee. Pass a task's non-empty `metadata.delivered_checks` and an accept may now name a commit whose effect is ABSENT at main HEAD — i.e. a landing that was later REVERTED, the exact task-1175 shape FIX 1' exists to catch. `escalation/src/escalation/git_authority.py` was the FIRST production call site ever to pass it (verified: `git show main:escalation/src/escalation/server.py | grep -c delivered_checks` -> 0).

WHY IT IS EASY TO MISS. The weakening is invisible on the returned object: `LandingEvidenceVerdict.accepted`/`.evidence_sha` are byte-identical either way, and a wrapper that discards `verdict.probe` on the accept path (as `_evidence_verdict` originally did) erases the only trace. The discriminant lives in `probe['delivered_checks_outcome']` and must be read by EQUALITY against `'confirmed'`, never truthiness: on a fully-guarded accept the key is ABSENT, and `'no_signal'`/`'disabled'`/the error case all return False from the differential and therefore reach `_reject`, so a truthiness test misreads `'no_signal'` as a rescue.

IT IS NARROW — three conjuncts, all required: the task declares a non-empty `metadata.delivered_checks`, fleet-wide `delivered_checks.enabled` is on, and the differential actually confirms. A task declaring nothing passes `[]`, which is falsy, so behaviour is unchanged for it.

WHAT TO DO WHEN YOU WIRE A SITE. Carry the rescue onto whatever your site returns, with the polarity "True means A GUARANTEE WAS WEAKENED" so the dataclass default is the safe reading, and give consumers ONE derived question rather than a list of flags to enumerate — `escalation/src/escalation/git_authority.py::GitAuthorityVerdict.merge_sha_fully_guarded` is the worked precedent (it folds `citation_gate_skipped` and `rescued_by_delivered_checks` into "may I stamp this sha as provenance as-is?", so a third weakening updates one expression instead of silently breaking every caller). Also re-read the prose around your site: any docstring or runbook asserting "the sha is effect-present-checked before being returned" becomes FALSE, and merge-queue's SKILL.md carried that claim in THREE spots, two of which authorize "accept it directly, do not re-check ancestry".

TESTING IT. Do NOT stub `validate_landing_evidence` to return a hand-built accepted verdict — that pins only your mapping and still passes if the second accept path is unreachable, which is the half that matters. Instead `monkeypatch.setattr('orchestrator.landing_evidence._delivered_checks_differential', <async stub>)` — the DEFINING module, because `validate_landing_evidence` resolves it as a module global and lazy per-call imports make any other patch target a no-op. The stub must set `probe['delivered_checks_outcome'] = 'confirmed'`, return True, and take `**kwargs` (the DISCOVERY arm passes an extra `anchor_is_branch_tip` the CANDIDATE arm does not). Pair every rescued-accept test with a negative control at `effect_present=True` and the SAME declared checks, or the flag silently degenerates into "this task declares delivered_checks".

Cause: aggressive_early_deflation sets `kwbot = kwtop.wrapping_sub(1)` (line 2222) when the deflation window starts at row 0, then computes `ihi - kwbot`. That wraps to the correct LAPACK value in release, but the generic QZ is monomorphised in reify-solver-elastic, which keeps dev overflow-checks on, so root `[profile.dev.package."*"]` overflow-checks=false does NOT help. Cheap reproducer: solve_eigen_dense on K=tridiag(-1,2,-1) n=136 with B tridiagonal (diag +1 for i<n/2, -0.5 after, off-diagonals 0.2). It passes with `cargo test --config 'profile.dev.package."reify-solver-elastic".overflow-checks=false'`. Task #7602 plans that profile override as the guard.
target_text: faer (0.24, used by reify-solver-elastic) is catastrophically slow in DEBUG builds because its SIMD numeric kernels (spread across faer + faer-traits + gemm/gemm-common/gemm-f64 + pulp + nano-gemm) run unoptimized with debug_assertions on — e.g. the n=80 shift-invert eigensolve is ~0.58s in release but 300-540s in debug (a ~500x debug-only pathology, NOT an algorithmic defect). The canonical remedy is a Cargo dev-profile dependency-optimization override in the ROOT workspace Cargo.toml (profiles in member manifests are silently ignored): `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 3` optimizes all third-party deps while keeping workspace crates at opt-level=0. A faer-only override is insufficient because the gemm/pulp crates stay slow. If opt-level=3 alone is not enough, also set debug-assertions=false / overflow-checks=false on the dep override. The one-time -O3 dep rebuild is amortized by the shared sccache.

entry_text: Measured 2026-10-03 (task 4076, base 4e76fbd912): when SpeculativeMergeWorker.stop() (orchestrator/src/orchestrator/merge_lane/worker.py) runs on a VERIFYING head, that head is released by three redundant paths: (1) stop()'s finalize-head arm; (2) stop()'s _inflight drain, because since task 5303 the head stays at _inflight[0] until its verify is done; (3) _finalize_inflight's finally, which releases the lease and permit when the verifier loop pops the cancelled head. Deleting only the arm's releases therefore leaks nothing. A mutation that takes the head off _inflight and drops its releases leaks all three resources. To build a head that really holds a speculation permit using public seams only: real GitOps, default speculation_depth=1, enqueue A then B with FakeVerifier scripts={A: dataclasses.replace(passes(), release=gate), B: hangs_until(ev)}, and wait for B 'awaiting_verify' with snapshot()['speculation']['inflight_speculative']==1 before opening A's gate. Observe the resources via snapshot()['hosts'][*]['slot_state'], ['owned_merge_worktrees'] plus on-disk existence, and ['speculation']['inflight_speculative']. The HostAllocator is real, built lazily by _ensure_host_allocator, so no fake _host_allocator is needed. A fake would also break test_merge_queue_restart_hook.py's ratchet private_reads=0.
target_text: SpeculativeMergeWorker._finalize_inflight (orchestrator/merge_queue.py) releases the host lease AND the speculation slot AND sets self._n_failed in a single `finally` block that runs on EVERY exit path including exceptions (respecting _skip_release / _cancel_release). Consequence for the verifier loop: the passthrough-finalize and finalize-head BaseException handlers must only resolve the Future + set _n_failed — they must NOT re-release lease/slot (finalize's finally already did). Only the pre-finalize dispatch handlers (input is a SpeculativeItem, no lease yet) and the head-failure cascade (guarded by the in-body _entry_released flag) actually own resource release. This is the invariant task ζ's _resolve_and_release(entry_or_item, outcome, *, chain_failed, release_resources, cancel_lease) chokepoint preserves via release_resources=False on the post-finalize paths.
